At an early median followup of 14 months
(1–36 months), there have been no late Grade 3 or greater
toxicity and only one patient had Grade 2 toxicity that con-
sisted of moderate subcutaneous induration/fibrosis. The
cosmetic outcome remains good to excellent in all patients.
There have been no ipsilateral breast recurrences. One
patient had regional nodal recurrence (without local recur-
rence) and 1 patient had a contralateral new breast primary.
There have been no distant recurrences.
For early-stage breast cancer, APBI is a convenient and
cost-effective option for appropriately selected patients.
Although a 10-fraction regimen delivered twice-daily over
1 week is most commonly used in North America,
delivering treatment in a shorter schedule is desirable.
Furthermore, a twice-daily fractionation schedule is not
convenient for most patients. In the initial prospective trial
evaluating the NIBB APBI technique, a dose of 34 Gy
delivered in 10 fractions was used (8, 9). The protocol al-
lowed for either twice-daily treatment over 1 week or
once-daily treatment over 2 weeks. The choice of
schedule was based solely on patient preference.
Seventy-three percent of patients elected to have once-
daily treatment despite a longer duration of 2 weeks. To

Several investigators are also exploring shorter schedule
treatments. Wilkinson et al. reported on 45 patients treated
with single-lumen intracavitary brachytherapy using a dose
of 28 Gy in four fractions (18). At 6 years followup, most
late toxicity was Grade 1–2 except for 1 patient with Grade
3 telangiectasia. Symptomatic seroma was seen in 13% and
rib fracture in 2 patients. The good-to-excellent cosmetic
outcome was 91%. The TRIUMPH-T trial is currently
ongoing with an accrual goal of 200 patients. This trial is
evaluating intracavitary brachytherapy to a dose of
22.5 Gy in three fractions using modern multilumen appli-
cators (19). Formenti et al. reported on APBI using a prone
3D-CRT technique with a dose of 30 Gy in five fractions.
The 5-year results for 100 patients have been reported
(20). Grade 3 toxicity was seen in 2% of patients, and

vival was 100%. Finally, the UK FAST trial is evaluating an

are randomized to either standard fractionation or to a
